He was an MP from 2014 to 2026, and the [[speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives]] from 2022 to 2023. Rurawhe held the seat for the [[Te Tai Hauāuru]] [[Māori electorates|Māori electorate]] from 2014 to 2023. Citing the demands of being speaker, he did not contest the electorate in the [[2023 New Zealand general election|2023 election]], but returned to Parliament at number 11 on Labour's party list. ==Background and professional career== Rurawhe was born in [[Taihape]] in 1961.{{cite web |url=https://www.parliament.nz/media/6305/roll-of-members-of-the-new-zealand-house-of-representatives-1854-onwards.pdf |title=Roll of members of the New Zealand House of Representatives, 1854 onwards |date=24 May 2019 |publisher=New Zealand Parliament |access-date=3 September 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201226033722/https://www.parliament.nz/media/6305/roll-of-members-of-the-new-zealand-house-of-representatives-1854-onwards.pdf |archive-date=26 December 2020 |url-status=live}}{{Cite web |last=Smith |first=Phil |date=16 October 2022 |title=Adrian Rurawhe: The accidental Speaker |url=https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/556051/adrian-rurawhe-the-accidental-speaker |access-date=30 September 2026 |website=RNZ |quote=Adrian Rurawhe is of Ngāti Apa iwi, but was born and raised outside their Manawatū/Whanganui heartland, in Taihape, (...)}} His parents were Wereta and Mihi Rurawhe, and his paternal grandparents were Paki and Meipara Rurawhe.{{cite news |first= Thomas |last= Couglan |date=30 September 2026 |title=Former Speaker of the House and Labour MP Adrian Rurawhe dies |url= https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/former-speaker-of-the-house-and-labour-mp-adrian-rurawhe-dies/664Z5QDSPZASBGDQGQLAMPAHTY/ |newspaper=[[The New Zealand Herald]] |access-date=1 October 2026}} His maternal grandparents were [[Matiu Rātana|Matiu]] and [[Iriaka Rātana]], who were both Members of Parliament for the [[Western Maori]] electorate between 1945 and 1969. He was a great-grandson of [[Rātana]] founder [[T. W. Ratana]].{{cite news |url=http://www.nzherald.co.nz/wanganui-chronicle/news/article.cfm?c_id=1503426&objectid=11173660 |title=Rurawhe new Labour candidate |work=[[Wanganui Chronicle]] |date=17 December 2013 |access-date=2 October 2014 |first=Laurel |last=Stowell |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006092747/http://www.nzherald.co.nz/wanganui-chronicle/news/article.cfm?c_id=1503426&objectid=11173660 |archive-date=6 October 2014 |url-status=dead}} His grandfather died before he was born, and he was at secondary school before he was aware that his "Nan" had been a Member of Parliament.{{cite news |title= Vision, values, philosophy guided by Ratana |first=Andrea |last=O'Neil |date=31 January 2015 |newspaper=[[The Post (New Zealand newspaper)|Dominion Post]]}} He had a background in health and education. He was the chairman of the [[Ngāti Apa]] [[Māori people|Māori]] [[iwi]] (tribe) for ten years and was on the team that negotiated the 2011 [[Treaty of Waitangi claims and settlements|treaty settlement]] with [[the Crown]] through the [[Waitangi Tribunal]].{{cite web|title=Settlement|url=http://www.ngatiapa.iwi.nz/settlement.html|publisher=[[Ngāti Apa]]|access-date=2 October 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141006090106/http://www.ngatiapa.iwi.nz/settlement.html|archive-date=6 October 2014|url-status=live}} [[Koro Wētere]], the former [[Eastern Maori]] MP, 2014–2017=== At the {{NZ election link|2014}}, after Turia had retired from politics, Rurawhe contested the [[Te Tai Hauāuru]] electorate for Labour and defeated Chris McKenzie of the Māori Party.{{cite news|last=Grocott|first=Matthew|url= http://www.stuff.co.nz/manawatu-standard/news/10528506/Rurawhe-regains-seat-for-Labour |title= Rurawhe regains seat for Labour |publisher=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=27 September 2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181025031230/http://www.stuff.co.nz/manawatu-standard/news/10528506/Rurawhe-regains-seat-for-Labour|archive-date=25 October 2018}} In his first term of Parliament, Labour was in [[Official Opposition (New Zealand)|Opposition]] and Rurawhe was appointed the Labour Party spokesperson for civil defence and emergency management (2014–2015), internal affairs (2015–2017) and Treaty of Waitangi negotiations (2017). He was also briefly junior whip after the [[2017 New Zealand Labour Party leadership election|election of Jacinda Ardern as Labour Party leader]] in 2017.{{cite web |title=Rt Hon Adrian Rurawhe |url= https://www3.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/rurawhe-adrian/ |publisher=New Zealand Parliament |access-date=3 October 2026 |date=16 March 2026}} In July 2015, Rurawhe introduced the Official Information (Parliamentary Under-Secretaries) Amendment Bill. Under the provisions of the bill, information held by parliamentary under-secretaries would be classified as official information and consequently subject to [[Official Information Act 1982|Official Information Act]] requests. The bill was passed into law with the support of all parties except [[New Zealand First]] and received royal assent in July 2016.{{Cite web|title=Official Information (Parliamentary Under-Secretaries) Amendment Bill – New Zealand Parliament|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL64530_1/official-information-parliamentary-under-secretaries|access-date=8 March 2021|website=www.parliament.nz|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220831050810/https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL64530_1/official-information-parliamentary-under-secretaries|archive-date=31 August 2022|url-status=live}} ===Second term, 2017–2020=== Rurawhe retained Te Tai Hauāuru for Labour in the [[2017 New Zealand general election|2017 general election]].{{cite web |url=http://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/75999049/te-tai-hauauru-mp-plans-to-stand-for-reelection-in-2017 |title= MP plans to stand for reelection in 2017 |work=[[Stuff (website)|Stuff]] |date=18 January 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181025031244/http://www.stuff.co.nz/taranaki-daily-news/75999049/te-tai-hauauru-mp-plans-to-stand-for-reelection-in-2017 |archive-date=25 October 2018|url-status=live}}{{cite web|title=Official Count Results – Te Tai Hauauru|url=http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-68.html|publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]]|access-date=24 December 2017|location=Wellington|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171224101748/http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-68.html|archive-date=24 December 2017|url-status=live}} Following the formation of the [[Sixth Labour Government of New Zealand|Sixth Labour Government]] in October 2017, Rurawhe was elected to the office of [[Speaker of the New Zealand House of Representatives#Deputies|assistant speaker]]. [[New Zealand National Party|National Party]] MP [[Simon Bridges]] challenged Rurawhe's election to the Chair on grounds that Rurawhe's name was still on the door of the [[Whip (politics)|whip]]'s office. Party whips are not eligible to be a presiding officer.{{Cite web |title=Standing Orders |url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/parliamentary-rules/standing-orders-2017-by-chapter/chapter-1-general-provisions-and-office-holders/ |access-date=5 May 2022 |website=Parliament.nz |language=en |quote=Standing Order 30: No member who is the leader of a party or who holds office as a whip may be appointed Deputy Speaker or Assistant Speaker.}} Speaker [[Trevor Mallard]] ruled that a name on a door in Parliament is not binding on the House and that the speaker's office had already been notified in writing that Rurawhe was not a whip, so the election could proceed.{{Cite web|url=https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/combined/HansD_20171108_20171108|title=Wednesday, 8 November 2017 – Volume 725|date=8 November 2017|publisher=[[New Zealand Parliament]]|access-date=9 November 2017|language=en|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181025041007/https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/combined/HansD_20171108_20171108|archive-date=25 October 2018}} ===Third term, 2020–2023=== Rurawhe won re-election in the [[2020 New Zealand general election|2020 general election]], defeating the Māori Party's candidate, [[Debbie Ngarewa-Packer]]. When the official results were released, Rurawhe had a majority of 1,035,{{cite web |title=Te Tai Hauāuru – Official Result |url=https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-69.html |publisher=[[Electoral Commission (New Zealand)|Electoral Commission]] |access-date=13 November 2020 Māori Party requested a recount in Te Tai Hauāuru, Rurawhe's majority increased slightly to 1,053.{{cite web |title=Amended Official Result for the Tāmaki Makaurau and Te Tai Hauāuru Electoral
